title: The report that was wrong
text:
My team lead asked me to prepare a weekly report about new users. I wrote a SQL query, ran it, and sent the numbers. Everybody was happy until Wednesday, when the sales manager called me. "Your report says we had 500 new users," he said. "But I count only 320."

I checked my query again. The reason was embarrassing but simple. Some users registered twice with different email addresses, and my query counted every row as a separate person. I also forgot to remove the test accounts that our developers create every day.

I fixed the query and added a filter for test accounts. I also wrote a short note under the report. It explained how I counted the users and which data I excluded. The manager liked it, because now he could trust the number and check it himself.

This story taught me an important thing about working with data. A query can run without errors and still give a wrong answer. Before you send a result, ask yourself one question: does this number make sense?

questions.prompt: Why was the number in the report too high?
options: The query counted duplicate registrations and test accounts.
The sales manager made a mistake.
The report was sent too late.
questions.explanation: Запит рахував кожен рядок як окрему людину, включно з повторними реєстраціями й тестовими акаунтами.

questions.prompt: What did the author add to make the report better?
options: A filter and a note about how users were counted
questions.explanation: Автор додав фільтр для тестових акаунтів і коротку примітку про те, як рахував.

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson of the story?
options: A query without errors can still give a wrong result.
questions.explanation: Запит може виконатися без помилок і все одно дати неправильну відповідь, тому результат варто перевіряти.
